strengths: Combining density-ratio-based optimization with graph-based label propagation and label spreading is a coherent, potentially useful contribution, particularly when a finite candidate pool provides geometry without additional objective evaluations. The paper appropriately acknowledges its foundations in BORE, LFBO, and established semi-supervised learning methods.

The evaluation covers synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and an image-derived search problem, with ten repeated runs and several relevant GP and classification-based baselines. The reported curves show competitive performance and substantial improvements in some settings, especially for label spreading.

The supplementary experiments investigate bandwidth, unlabeled sample count, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling. The comparison without unlabeled data is particularly useful evidence that adding these points can improve optimization beyond simply adopting a kernel classifier.
weaknesses: The theoretical conclusions in Section 4.3 are insufficiently supported. Sampling truncated Gaussians around observations does not guarantee the cluster assumption: high-density regions can cross the objective's good/bad boundary, which also changes across iterations. Equations (11)–(13) invoke existence results for classification learners without establishing their applicability to the proposed propagation algorithms or connecting classification error to optimization performance. Furthermore, 100 unlabeled points do not maintain the assumed condition n_u much greater than n_l over 500 evaluations. These arguments do not justify the superiority statement following Equation (8).

The central explanation involving overconfidence remains largely qualitative. Section 3.1 defines it through a small region receiving high positive-class probability, but a larger positive region does not itself imply more exploratory queries under acquisition maximization. Figures 1, s.1, and s.2 illustrate different prediction surfaces without measuring exclusion of promising regions or escape from local optima. The useful ablation in Figure s.5 covers only two functions and does not isolate the contributions of propagation, bandwidth, and randomized tie-breaking. Matched controls and quantitative exploration diagnostics would strengthen this principal claim.

Important experimental details are missing: the main experiments' bandwidth and clamping-factor settings or tuning procedures, feature normalization and categorical encoding, and subsample sizes for large pools. Candidate selection on discrete pools and acquisition optimization for the baselines are also unclear despite the stated use of 1,000 L-BFGS-B initializations. These omissions materially limit reproduction and assessment of comparison fairness, particularly because Figure s.4 demonstrates substantial bandwidth sensitivity.

The MNIST experiment provides limited evidence for black-box image optimization. Section S.3.4 constructs features using a network trained on 440,000 examples labeled with the exact three-digit target, achieving 96.9% test classification accuracy. This supplies extensive task-specific supervision before optimization begins. A baseline that ranks candidates using this network's own predictions, together with an explicit accounting of the supervision and preprocessing cost, is needed to establish the added value of the optimization procedure.

The continuous-sampling experiments use only two-dimensional functions, leaving performance in more demanding continuous spaces unresolved. Practical computational tradeoffs are also unquantified: dense graph construction requires quadratic storage in the combined labeled and unlabeled sample count, yet no runtime or memory results accompany the large-pool experiments. The subsampling study uses small synthetic pools. Random search would additionally provide a useful reference for the claimed exploration benefits.

Smaller presentation issues need correction. The definition p_ij = w_ij / sum_k w_kj implies P = W D^{-1}, whereas the text states P = D^{-1} W before using P transposed in Equation (6); the intended update should be unambiguous. The figures also need to define what their shaded uncertainty bands represent.
